stem: If v(t)=3t² in SI units, the acceleration at t=2 s is

rationales.A: Reads the coefficient 3 in v(t)=3t² as the acceleration itself, as if v were proportional to t, instead of differentiating v(t) with respect to time.
rationales.B: Mistakenly differentiates v(t)=3t² using an incomplete power rule (dropping the exponent multiplier), computing dv/dt=3t instead of the correct 6t, then evaluates 3(2)=6 m/s² at the correct time t=2 s.
rationales.C: dv/dt=6t, evaluated at t=2 s gives 12 m/s².
rationales.D: Multiplies 6t by t again instead of substituting t=2, giving 6t²=6(2)²=24.

stem: The displacement from t=0 to T for v(t)=kt is

rationales.A: Gives the final velocity v(T)=kT, which has units of speed rather than displacement; displacement requires integrating the linearly increasing velocity over the interval.
rationales.B: Integrates kt dt to kT² but drops the 1/2 factor that comes from the power rule.
rationales.D: Divides the constant k by T, a quantity with units of acceleration per unit time, instead of integrating the velocity over the interval; it is not a displacement.

stem: A force F(x)=ax acts in one dimension. The work from 0 to L is

rationales.A: Mistakes the endpoint force value F(L)=aL for the work itself, without multiplying by the displacement.
rationales.B: Multiplies the endpoint force F(L)=aL by the full distance L as if the force were constant, missing the 1/2 factor from integrating the linearly increasing force.
rationales.C: the integral of ax dx is aL²/2
rationales.D: Divides the force gradient a by L instead of integrating the force over the displacement; integrating ax always produces a term proportional to L², never a/L.

stem: A particle moves in one dimension under a conservative force with potential energy U(x). The force on the particle is given by which of the following?

rationales.A: Drops the negative sign, forgetting that force opposes (rather than follows) the direction of increasing potential energy.
rationales.B: force is the negative potential gradient
rationales.C: Divides U by x instead of differentiating; -U/x equals -dU/dx only when U is directly proportional to x, so it is wrong for a general potential energy function.
rationales.D: This differentiates U twice. The second derivative is the curvature (stiffness) of the potential well and equals minus the rate of change of the force with position; it is not the force itself, which is −dU/dx.

stem: A power law P(t)=ct² delivers energy from 0 to T equal to

rationales.A: Evaluates the power at time T and treats that instantaneous value as the total energy, without integrating over the interval.
rationales.B: Integrates ct² correctly in form but uses the wrong power-rule denominator, writing t³/2 instead of t³/3.
rationales.C: energy is the time integral of power
rationales.D: Differentiates P(t)=ct² instead of integrating it, computing d/dt(ct²)=2ct and evaluating at T.

stem: At a stable equilibrium x₀, U(x) has

rationales.C: Assumes equilibrium requires the slope to blow up rather than vanish, misreading dU/dx=0 as an undefined or infinite condition.
rationales.D: Assumes equilibrium points must be non-smooth kinks in U(x) rather than smooth minima where dU/dx=0.

rationales.A: differentiate position with respect to time
rationales.B: Drops the coefficient 3 that the power rule brings down from At³, reducing the exponent without multiplying by it.
rationales.C: Reduces the exponent on At³ by one too many, an off-by-one power-rule slip giving t instead of t².
rationales.D: Gives only the cubic term At³ and drops the −Bt term; no derivative has been taken, so this is not a velocity expression at all.

stem: A force F(x)=F₀e^{-x/L} acts along the direction of displacement, with L a positive constant. The work done as the object moves from x=0 to x→∞ is

rationales.A: Inverts the decay length, dividing by L instead of multiplying, as if the integral shrank rather than scaled by the decay length.
rationales.B: The integral ∫₀^∞ F₀e^{-x/L}dx = F₀L converges because L>0 makes the exponential decay (not grow) as x increases.
rationales.C: Assumes the force decaying to zero as x→∞ means the enclosed area (work) also vanishes, rather than converging to a finite nonzero value.
rationales.D: Assumes an infinite integration limit must always produce infinite work, missing that the exponential integrand decays fast enough to converge.

rationales.A: This is the first derivative, velocity, rather than acceleration.
rationales.B: Two time derivatives give v=4Ct³ and a=12Ct².
rationales.C: This differentiates a third time, one differentiation too many: d³x/dt³ = 24Ct.
rationales.D: This reduces the exponent without applying the power-rule coefficients.

stem: The signed area under a velocity-versus-time graph equals

rationales.A: Acceleration is the slope of velocity versus time, not its area.
rationales.B: The time integral of velocity is the signed change in position.
rationales.C: Distance traveled adds all areas as positive, but signed velocity-time area gives displacement.
rationales.D: Change in velocity comes from integrating acceleration, not velocity.

stem: For U(x)=(1/2)kx² with k>0, x=0 is stable because

rationales.A: The potential has positive curvature and a local minimum at equilibrium.
rationales.B: A local maximum corresponds to unstable equilibrium.
rationales.C: The force -kx varies with position and is not constant.
rationales.D: The chosen potential is nonnegative and energy sign is not the stability criterion.

stem: For m dv/dt=-bv, the characteristic decay time is

rationales.A: This is the decay rate with units of inverse time, not the time constant.
rationales.B: The solution e^{-bt/m} has time constant τ=m/b.
rationales.C: This confuses the velocity-decay time with the faster decay time of kinetic energy.
rationales.D: This is the half-life, not the characteristic velocity-decay time m/b.

stem: A particle in uniform circular motion has

rationales.A: This confuses constant speed with zero acceleration.
rationales.B: The velocity vector rotates continuously and is not constant.
rationales.C: Its changing velocity direction requires inward acceleration v²/r.
rationales.D: The net force is inward; an outward force is not required in an inertial frame.

stem: The work done from x=a to x=b by F(x) is

rationales.A: Mechanical work along x is the position integral of force over the path.
rationales.B: This assumes the final force acts constantly over the entire displacement.
rationales.C: Averaging the endpoint forces is not valid for every F(x); it equals the integral only in special cases such as a force that is linear in position, so the word 'always' makes this false.
rationales.D: A time integral of force is impulse, not work.

rationales.B: The negative spatial derivative gives F=-dU/dx=-3Ax².
rationales.C: This keeps the negative sign but omits the power-rule factor three.
rationales.D: This divides by the exponent instead of multiplying by it when differentiating Ax³.

stem: At a one-dimensional classical turning point with total energy E,

rationales.A: Potential zero depends on reference choice and is not the turning criterion.
rationales.B: At a turning point K=0, so total energy equals potential energy.
rationales.C: Force can be nonzero at a turning point and reverse the motion.
rationales.D: Kinetic energy is zero rather than maximum at the turning point.

stem: A force F acts on a particle with velocity v. Instantaneous power is

rationales.A: Instantaneous mechanical power is the scalar product F·v.
rationales.B: A cross product gives a vector and does not represent energy-transfer rate.
rationales.C: This ignores the angle between force and velocity; only the parallel force component contributes to power.
rationales.D: Power is the rate of work, F·v; the product of force and acceleration F·a does not have units of power and is not the rate of energy transfer.
